name: Half-face respirators, cartridges and filters
summary: A reusable rubber or silicone mask over nose and mouth that takes particle filters for dust and gas or vapour cartridges for solvents and other vapours.
uses: Dust, mould spores, fibreglass, asbestos and lead with P100 (magenta) or P3 filters; for asbestos at work, OSHA wants this rather than a disposable (CDC mould clean-up)
Airborne germs from dusty droppings or nests, with P100 or P3 filters; it guards only your airways, not your skin or eyes
Solvent and paint vapour with organic vapour cartridges (black; brown A in Europe); acid gas, chlorine, ammonia or mercury vapour only with the cartridge made for that gas
Cartridges give no reliable warning when spent: change them on a schedule, and leave if you smell or taste the chemical (mercury has no smell)
Ordinary cartridges don't stop carbon monoxide, and no filter mask works in oxygen-poor air: silos, tanks, pits, sewers, wells, fires
Doesn't protect the eyes; seals only on a clean-shaven face
identify: A soft rubber or silicone facepiece over nose and mouth, with a head harness, an outlet valve and one or two filter sockets. The colour tells you what a cartridge stops. US cartridge colours: black organic vapour, white acid gas, green ammonia, yellow organic vapour plus acid gas, magenta (purple) P100 particle filter; combination cartridges show both colours (OSHA bulletin; CDPR colours). For multi-gas, OSHA's bulletin and California's chart differ (brown, olive or olive/brown), so go by the protections printed on the cartridge, not its colour. 42 CFR 84.193 requires the colours to follow ANSI K13.1-1973 but does not list them (42 CFR 84.193). US particle filters are N (not oil-resistant), R (oil-resistant) or P (oil-proof) at 95, 99 or 100 (99.97%) efficiency (NIOSH construction dust; NIOSH FFR page). Europe: brown A organic vapour, brown AX low-boiling organics, grey B inorganic gas (not carbon monoxide), yellow E acid gas, green K ammonia, red-and-white Hg mercury, white P particles, gas filters carry a capacity class 1 (low) to 3 (high) and particle filters an efficiency class P1 (low), P2 (medium) or P3 (high), so A2P3 is a medium-capacity organic vapour filter with a P3 particle filter (HSE HSG53). A genuine cartridge shows the maker, part number, protection type, NIOSH and a lot number. Fakes reuse real 3M part numbers such as 60921 and 60926 and claim to fit 3M's 6000, 7000 and FF-400 masks (NIOSH counterfeit cartridges). The full approval label is a paper sheet in the box listing the mask, cartridges and parts approved together, with TC-23C numbers for gas sets and TC-84A for particle or combination sets; parts not on it can cause serious injury or death (NIOSH approval labels). US gas cartridges are approved only for air that is not immediately dangerous, up to limits such as 1,000 ppm organic vapour or 10 ppm chlorine (42 CFR 84.190). In Canada, look for NIOSH or CSA approval (Alberta producers).
test: Before each use, check the facepiece is soft and springy, not sticky, cracked or warped; the straps stretch and buckles hold; and the valves are present, flat and seated. Perished or warped valves can't seal (OSHA 1910.134; HSE HSG53). Fit two identical filters to a twin-filter mask (HSE HSG53). Gas cartridges should come from an air-tight pack and be within date: OSHA says even cartridges in their original packaging have expiry dates, and open ones, or ones not in air-tight packaging, should not be used (OSHA bulletin). Particle filters past their expiry date should not be used either (HSE HSG53). Seal check every time. Negative: palms or a thin glove over the inlets, breathe in gently so the mask pulls in, hold about 10 seconds; it must stay pulled in. Positive: cover the outlet valve and breathe out gently; pressure should build up slightly inside the mask with no air leaking out at the edge (OSHA seal check). A seal check is not a fit test (NIOSH FFR page). Change particle filters when breathing gets hard or they are damaged or dirty (NIOSH cartridge life). Change gas cartridges on a schedule, not by smell (OSHA change schedules): HSE suggests class 1 at least every two days (daily for cancer- or asthma-causing chemicals), class 2 weekly, Hg after 50 hours at most, AX after one use, and at once if you smell or taste anything (HSE HSG53). NIOSH describes mercury as odourless (NIOSH mercury guide), so for mercury go by the time limit, not smell. After use, clean and disinfect the mask and store it away from sun, heat, damp, dust and chemicals, packed so the facepiece and valves don't warp (OSHA 1910.134).

decay.note: Estimate: NIOSH's example gives a reusable facepiece ten years and a particle filter five (NIOSH shelf life); no maker figure for cartridges was found. OSHA says cartridges carry expiry dates and opened ones shouldn't be used (OSHA bulletin), so cartridges run out first.

improvise: No half mask: a P100 or FFP3 disposable covers particle jobs but not vapour (NIOSH FFR page); for asbestos at work, OSHA bars disposables and requires HEPA filters on a half mask or better (OSHA asbestos). For airborne germs, such as dust from rodent droppings and nests, CDC lists a half mask with HEPA filters for heavy infestations, with goggles and gloves; the mask guards only the airways (CDC rodent clean-up). Don't trust a homemade charcoal filter: even a real cartridge gives no protection once full, and its life is hard to predict (HSE HSG53), so one of unknown capacity is a gamble. Particle filters don't stop vapour, including mercury vapour, which needs its own cartridge (HSE HSG53). Don't mix brands: a cartridge or filter that is not on the mask's approval label is outside the approval, and NIOSH warns that parts not on the label can cause serious injury or death (NIOSH approval labels; NIOSH counterfeit cartridges). A seal check only shows the mask seals on your face (OSHA seal check), not that the filter works. Diisocyanate vapours (TDI, HDI, MDI) can damage the eyes and few cartridges warn when spent, so a half mask needs eye or face protection and some jobs need an air-fed mask (OSHA isocyanate letter). For beryllium dust, the NIOSH Pocket Guide lists full-face masks or better (NIOSH beryllium guide). Bearded: shave the seal line; only loose-fitting hooded respirators, usually battery-powered, work with beards (CDC fit testing; NIOSH construction dust). Never enter a silo, manure pit, tank, sewer, well or burning building in one: no filter mask works in oxygen-poor air (HSE HSG53; Alberta producers). Ordinary cartridges don't stop carbon monoxide: grey B filters are marked not for CO (HSE HSG53), and CO needs special filters most masks lack (OSHA bulletin).
